newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai business awaits economic lift from Chavalit.
newsitem.headline: Thai business awaits economic lift from Chavalit.

text.p: Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, set to become Thailand's new prime minister, will have to act quickly to bolster the economy to counter concern among businessmen that his coalition government will be weak, analysts said on Tuesday.

Chavalit was nominated by his five coalition partners to be prime minister after his New Aspiration Party (NAP) won 125 seats in parliament in Sunday's election, two more than the rival Democrat Party.

"The tenure of the new coalition depends on its performance (in handling the economy), which could help offset its overall poor image held by the business sector in Bangkok," said Suchit Bunbongkarn of Chulalongkorn University.
If Chavalit fails to get results quickly, public and investor confidence in the new government and the economy would deteriorate further, analysts said.
They acknowledged that Chavalit had made a good move in enlisting the Chart Pattana Party (CPP), which is experienced in business, as a coalition partner.
The CPP, headed by former premier Chatichai Choonhavan, would boost Chavalit's economic team by providing cabinet ministers well versed in economic affairs, they said.

Chavalit said Amnuay Viravan, caretaker deputy premier and a former Bangkok Bank executive chairman, was widely expected to fill the finance post. He would lead a small team to help Chavalit reverse the slowing of Thailand's economy this year.
Pisarn Manoleehagul, president of Thai Farmers Research Center Co Ltd, was sceptical that an Amnuay-led team could work smoothly with elected politicians in Chavalit's cabinet.
"His economic dream team will fail to perform to expectations if it does not have a free hand," he said.

The Thai economy is projected to expand by slightly more than six percent in 1996, its slowest rate in 10 years. Exports are projected to rise three to five percent this year against 23.6 percent growth in 1995.
Analysts said time may be on Chavalit's side, however.

"The economic slowdown seems to have bottomed out with inflation and the current account deficit showing improving signs in the past two months," said Somjai Phagaphasvivat, a Thammasat University lecturer.
Thailand's financial and stock markets waited for Chavalit to keep his campaign pledge to name non-elected experts to key economic portfolios.
The stock index was cheered by the news of the CPP's joining the coalition and closed up 21.85 points, or 2.32 percent, at 964.19 on Tuesday, after a 5.8 percent tumble on Monday.

Suchit Bunbongkarn, dean of political sciences at Chulalongkorn University, said: "I have detected signs of Chavalit reneging on his campaign pledge to bring in outside experts. His partners now talk about quotas on cabinet jobs based on party strength."
Analysts said that allocating cabinet posts by quota would compromise NAP's election promise of leaving economic management to experts and keeping it from political interference.

A major challenge for Chavalit would be maintaining factional unity within his expanded NAP, analysts said. But Thammasat's Somjai said he expected Chavalit to keep his coalition in line at least for the first three months in office.

"I think we have under-estimated him," Somjai said of Chavalit. "He has proved a good strategist since he was in the army. I don't think he has come this far by accident. The decision to include CPP in his cabinet showed that he was in touch with public and business opinions."
Suchit said Chavalit would also have to overcome public suspicion of his having backed big military spending in the past when he was defence minister.
